The IFN-associated pattern label is read from each implementation’s source table rather than typed by hand. The saved R result labels the IFN-associated pattern Pattern4; the saved Python-compatible result labels the corresponding signal Pattern5. The static figure files displayed in the narrative use the selected R model as the primary evidence source, but the R and Python code tabs below read their own implementation-specific source tables.

Pattern numbers are therefore run-specific. The source tables also carry cautious working labels, such as “IFN-associated stimulation” or “monocyte-linked.” Treat those labels as interpretation guides to check, not as names that were known before the analysis.

Screen Patterns Before Naming Them

Start with a pattern-level screen. The left panel compares each pattern’s activity with the control-versus-IFN-beta stimulation label. The right panel asks the same question in a more concrete way: for each pattern, how far apart are the average control and stimulated activities?

This is a useful first look because it prevents you from naming a pattern only by its top genes. If a pattern is truly stimulation-associated, you should also see its cell activity shift toward IFN-beta-stimulated cells.

The code below reconstructs the first panel from the source table. In R, arrange() orders the rows by the stimulation correlation, and mutate() creates a learner-facing y-axis label that combines the pattern number with its working interpretation. In Python, sort_values() performs the same ordering step, and a new pattern_display column provides the same combined label. The plotting code then draws a line from zero to each correlation value, with the IFN-associated candidate highlighted.

  • R
  • Python
pattern_screen_r <- pattern_condition_r |>
  dplyr::arrange(corr_with_stim) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    pattern_display = paste0(pattern, "\n", working_label),
    pattern_display = factor(pattern_display, levels = pattern_display)
  )

ggplot(
  pattern_screen_r,
  aes(x = corr_with_stim, y = pattern_display, color = is_ifn_candidate)
) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey80") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = corr_with_stim, yend = pattern_display), linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#64748B", "TRUE" = "#E76F51"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Pattern activity compared with IFN-beta stimulation",
    x = "Correlation with stimulation",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
plot_data = pattern_condition.sort_values("corr_with_stim")
plot_data = plot_data.assign(
    pattern_display=plot_data["pattern"] + "\n" + plot_data["working_label"]
)
colors = plot_data["is_ifn_candidate"].map({True: "#E76F51", False: "#64748B"})

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.8))
ax.axvline(0, color="0.8")
ax.hlines(
    y=plot_data["pattern_display"],
    xmin=0,
    xmax=plot_data["corr_with_stim"],
    color=colors,
    linewidth=4,
)
ax.scatter(plot_data["corr_with_stim"], plot_data["pattern_display"], color=colors, s=80)
ax.set_xlabel("Correlation with stimulation")
ax.set_ylabel("")
ax.set_title("Pattern activity compared with IFN-beta stimulation")
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The screen points to one strong positive stimulation-associated pattern in each saved implementation: Pattern4 in the selected R run and Pattern5 in the saved Python-compatible run. A second pattern also has positive association with stimulation, but the IFN-associated candidate is much stronger by this metric. You should still avoid treating this plot as a final answer. It tells you where to look next.

Compare Pattern Activity With Cell Neighborhoods

The pattern screen tells you which pattern is most associated with stimulation, but it does not show where the activity sits in the cell population. For that, it helps to use the as a reference map. A UMAP is not the CoGAPS model itself; it is a two-dimensional layout of the cells that you can recolor in different ways.

In the paired UMAPs below, the left panel is always the same annotated PBMC identity map. The right panel recolors those same cells by one CoGAPS pattern. This lets you ask a visual question that a summary table cannot answer as directly: does the activity appear across several PBMC neighborhoods, or is it concentrated in one immune-cell region?

The IFN-associated pattern is included, but it is not the only pattern worth inspecting. Some patterns are more identity-linked, meaning their strongest activity sits mainly in one annotated neighborhood such as monocytes or T cells. The caption for each figure gives a cautious working interpretation based on the selected-model summaries. Comparing several patterns side by side teaches an important habit: a latent-variable model should be read as a collection of partially overlapping signals, not as a single treatment-response plot.

  • Pattern 1
  • Pattern 2
  • Pattern 3
  • Pattern 4
  • Pattern 5
  • Pattern 6

The code below shows how one paired UMAP comparison is built from the long UMAP source table. The first plot maps cell_type to color, so you can see the annotated PBMC neighborhoods. The second plot keeps the same umap_1 and umap_2 coordinates but maps activity to color for one CoGAPS pattern.

In R, filter() keeps one pattern at a time, and arrange(activity) draws low-activity cells first so high-activity cells are not hidden underneath them. In Python, the same logic uses Boolean filtering and sort_values(). In both languages, the useful programming idea is the same: once the data are in a tidy table, changing the color variable changes the biological layer you are viewing without changing the cell positions.

  • R
  • Python
pattern_to_map_r <- ifn_pattern_for_visuals_r

umap_one_pattern_r <- pattern_umap_r |>
  dplyr::filter(pattern == pattern_to_map_r) |>
  dplyr::arrange(activity)

cell_type_colors_r <- c(
  "CD4 T cells" = "#2A9D8F",
  "CD14+ Monocytes" = "#457B9D",
  "B cells" = "#E9C46A",
  "NK cells" = "#7E68B1",
  "CD8 T cells" = "#52B788",
  "FCGR3A+ Monocytes" = "#F4A261",
  "Dendritic cells" = "#5B6770",
  "Megakaryocytes" = "#D1495B"
)

identity_umap_r <- ggplot(
  umap_one_pattern_r,
  aes(x = umap_1, y = umap_2, color = cell_type)
) +
  geom_point(size = 0.45, alpha = 0.72) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = cell_type_colors_r,
    name = "Cell type",
    guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 4, alpha = 1))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Identity reference",
    subtitle = "Each point is one cell; color shows the annotated PBMC identity.",
    x = "UMAP 1",
    y = "UMAP 2"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

activity_umap_r <- ggplot(
  umap_one_pattern_r,
  aes(x = umap_1, y = umap_2, color = activity)
) +
  geom_point(size = 0.45, alpha = 0.72) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_gradientn(
    colors = c("#1F2937", "#6D3A9C", "#E76F51", "#FDE68A"),
    name = "Pattern activity"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste(pattern_to_map_r, "activity on the PBMC UMAP"),
    subtitle = "The same UMAP coordinates can be recolored by any CoGAPS pattern.",
    x = "UMAP 1",
    y = "UMAP 2"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

identity_umap_r
activity_umap_r
pattern_to_map = ifn_pattern_for_visuals

umap_one_pattern = (
    pattern_umap.loc[pattern_umap["pattern"].eq(pattern_to_map)]
    .sort_values("activity")
)

cell_type_colors = {
    "CD4 T cells": "#2A9D8F",
    "CD14+ Monocytes": "#457B9D",
    "B cells": "#E9C46A",
    "NK cells": "#7E68B1",
    "CD8 T cells": "#52B788",
    "FCGR3A+ Monocytes": "#F4A261",
    "Dendritic cells": "#5B6770",
    "Megakaryocytes": "#D1495B",
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=2, figsize=(7.4, 9.6), constrained_layout=True)

for cell_type, group in umap_one_pattern.groupby("cell_type"):
    axes[0].scatter(
        group["umap_1"],
        group["umap_2"],
        color=cell_type_colors.get(cell_type, "0.6"),
        s=3,
        alpha=0.72,
        linewidths=0,
        label=cell_type,
    )
axes[0].set_title("Identity reference")
axes[0].set_xlabel("UMAP 1")
axes[0].set_ylabel("UMAP 2")
axes[0].set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
axes[0].legend(
    title="Cell type",
    loc="center left",
    bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5),
    frameon=False,
    markerscale=3,
)

scatter = axes[1].scatter(
    umap_one_pattern["umap_1"],
    umap_one_pattern["umap_2"],
    c=umap_one_pattern["activity"],
    cmap="magma",
    s=3,
    alpha=0.72,
    linewidths=0,
)
axes[1].set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
axes[1].set_xlabel("UMAP 1")
axes[1].set_ylabel("UMAP 2")
axes[1].set_title(f"{pattern_to_map} activity on the PBMC UMAP")
fig.colorbar(scatter, ax=axes[1], label="Pattern activity")
<matplotlib.colorbar.Colorbar object at 0x7fffb3b1be80>
plt.show()

The paired UMAPs show why it would be too narrow to visualize only the IFN-associated pattern. Pattern 4 has broad stimulation-associated activity, but other patterns are visibly concentrated in particular immune-cell neighborhoods. That does not automatically name those patterns biologically; it gives you a visual hypothesis to test later with cell-type summaries, top genes, and directionality.

Check Whether The Shift Is Paired Across Donors

The source study used a : each donor contributed control and IFN-beta-stimulated aliquots. A useful visualization should respect that design. Instead of treating all control cells and all stimulated cells as unrelated groups, the next figure computes a within-donor difference:

mean stimulated activity - mean control activity

Positive values mean that the IFN-associated pattern is more active in the stimulated aliquot from that same donor.

The code uses a wide table with one row per donor and separate columns for control and stimulated mean activity. The important programming move is creating and plotting stim_minus_ctrl, a new column that stores the paired difference. In R, geom_segment() draws each difference from zero to its observed value. In Python, ax.hlines() does the same thing.

  • R
  • Python
ggplot(replicate_pairs_r) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = 0, xend = stim_minus_ctrl, y = donor_label, yend = donor_label),
    color = "#F2B7A4",
    linewidth = 3.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = stim_minus_ctrl, y = donor_label), color = "#E76F51", size = 3.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(replicate_pairs_r$stim_minus_ctrl), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Donor-paired shifts in IFN-associated activity",
    x = "Mean activity difference (IFN-beta - control)",
    y = "Matched donor pair"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.8))
y = np.arange(len(replicate_pairs))
ax.axvline(0, color="0.8")
ax.hlines(
    y,
    xmin=0,
    xmax=replicate_pairs["stim_minus_ctrl"],
    color="#F2B7A4",
    linewidth=6,
)
ax.scatter(replicate_pairs["stim_minus_ctrl"], y, color="#E76F51", s=70)
ax.axvline(replicate_pairs["stim_minus_ctrl"].mean(), color="#0B2239", linestyle="--")
ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(replicate_pairs["donor_label"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel("Mean activity difference (IFN-beta - control)")
ax.set_ylabel("Matched donor pair")
ax.set_title("Donor-paired shifts in IFN-associated activity")
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The paired view is reassuring because the stimulation-associated increase is not driven by a single donor. In both saved implementations, each donor has higher mean activity after IFN-beta stimulation than in the matched control aliquot for the implementation-specific IFN-associated pattern. This does not replace a formal donor-aware statistical model, but it is an important visual check before making a biological interpretation.

Compare Activity Across PBMC Identities

PBMCs contain several immune-cell types, so the next question is whether the IFN-associated pattern is only a marker of one annotated identity or whether it cuts across the mixture. The plot below summarizes mean activity by annotated PBMC identity and condition.

The source table has one row per cell type and columns for the mean control activity, mean stimulated activity, and the difference. The R code orders cell types by stimulated activity so the strongest stimulated groups appear at the top. The Python code uses the same ordering and draws a horizontal line from control to stimulated activity for each cell type.

  • R
  • Python
celltype_plot_r <- celltype_condition_r |>
  dplyr::arrange(stim) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell_type = factor(cell_type, levels = cell_type))

ggplot(celltype_plot_r, aes(y = cell_type)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = ctrl, xend = stim, yend = cell_type), color = "grey82", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = ctrl), color = "#64748B", size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = stim), color = "#E76F51", size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "IFN-associated activity by PBMC identity",
    x = "Mean pattern activity",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
celltype_plot = celltype_condition.sort_values("stim")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 5.2))
y = np.arange(len(celltype_plot))
ax.hlines(y, celltype_plot["ctrl"], celltype_plot["stim"], color="0.82", linewidth=3)
ax.scatter(celltype_plot["ctrl"], y, color="#64748B", s=70, label="control")
ax.scatter(celltype_plot["stim"], y, color="#E76F51", s=70, label="IFN-beta, 6 h")
ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(celltype_plot["cell_type"])
ax.set_xlabel("Mean pattern activity")
ax.set_title("IFN-associated activity by PBMC identity")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Most annotated PBMC identities show higher mean activity in IFN-beta-stimulated cells, which supports a broad stimulation-associated interpretation. The heights are not identical, however. FCGR3A+ monocytes, B cells, NK cells, and dendritic cells show especially high stimulated activity, while megakaryocytes remain low. That is the kind of pattern you should expect in single-cell data: a shared response can still vary by cell type.

Look For Shared And Cell-Type-Linked Structure

The IFN-associated pattern is only one part of the selected model. Other patterns may track monocytes, antigen-presentation structure, baseline lymphocyte structure, or other sources of variation. A heatmap is useful here because it lets you scan all patterns and cell types at once.

The color scale below shows one subtraction for each pattern and annotated PBMC identity: mean activity in IFN-beta-stimulated cells minus mean activity in control cells. A positive value means that pattern is stronger, on average, after stimulation; those tiles are red. A negative value means that pattern is stronger, on average, in the matched control cells; those tiles are blue. Values close to zero are pale because the two conditions have similar mean activity for that pattern and cell type.

The code uses the same source table as the heatmap. In R, geom_tile() maps one shift value to one heatmap cell, and geom_text() prints the rounded shift value on top of each tile. In Python, pivot() reshapes the table so rows are patterns, columns are cell types, and values are condition shifts; the loop after imshow() then writes the rounded value into each tile. Those printed numbers are useful because color shows direction and strength quickly, while the value tells you the actual size of the shift.

  • R
  • Python
ggplot(
  pattern_celltype_shift_r,
  aes(x = cell_type, y = pattern, fill = stim_minus_ctrl)
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(stim_minus_ctrl, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2B8CBE",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#E76F51",
    midpoint = 0,
    name = "stim - control"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Condition shifts by pattern and cell type",
    x = "Annotated PBMC identity",
    y = "CoGAPS pattern"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))
heatmap_matrix = pattern_celltype_shift.pivot(
    index="pattern",
    columns="cell_type",
    values="stim_minus_ctrl",
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.2))
vmax = np.abs(heatmap_matrix.to_numpy()).max()
im = ax.imshow(heatmap_matrix, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax, aspect="auto")
for row_idx in range(heatmap_matrix.shape[0]):
    for col_idx in range(heatmap_matrix.shape[1]):
        value = heatmap_matrix.iloc[row_idx, col_idx]
        label = "0.00" if abs(value) < 0.005 else f"{value:.2f}"
        text_color = "white" if abs(value) > vmax * 0.65 else "#0B2239"
        ax.text(col_idx, row_idx, label, ha="center", va="center", color=text_color, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(heatmap_matrix.shape[1]))
ax.set_xticklabels(heatmap_matrix.columns, rotation=35, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(heatmap_matrix.shape[0]))
ax.set_yticklabels(heatmap_matrix.index)
ax.set_title("Condition shifts by pattern and cell type")
ax.set_xlabel("Annotated PBMC identity")
ax.set_ylabel("CoGAPS pattern")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="stim - control")
<matplotlib.colorbar.Colorbar object at 0x7fffb3a471f0>
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This view helps separate broad stimulation structure from more cell-type-linked behavior. Read each row as one CoGAPS pattern and each column as one annotated PBMC identity. If a row is red across many columns, that pattern is broadly stronger after stimulation. If a row has strong color in only one or two columns, that pattern may be more tied to particular immune-cell identities. Negative blue values are not “bad” model behavior; they tell you that the pattern’s mean activity is higher in controls for that cell type. That contrast is important because CoGAPS is learning multiple overlapping patterns, not a single treatment-versus-control axis.

Connect Top Genes To Direction

The last visualization combines two pieces of evidence that are easy to confuse. A high CoGAPS gene weight means a gene helps define a pattern. It does not say whether the gene is higher in stimulation. For that, you need a separate expression-direction summary.

The saved figure below shows the selected R run, where the IFN-associated pattern is Pattern4. The Python tab below uses the same check for the Python saved output, where the corresponding IFN-associated pattern is Pattern5.

The R code below uses ifelse() to choose a color from the direction column. The Python code uses map() for the same purpose. Both versions show the key idea: first rank genes by pattern weight, then check whether each gene rises or falls in the stimulation contrast.

  • R
  • Python
gene_direction_plot_r <- top_gene_direction_r |>
  dplyr::arrange(desc(rank)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    gene = factor(gene, levels = gene),
    direction_color = ifelse(direction == "up_in_stim", "higher in stimulation", "lower in stimulation")
  )

ggplot(gene_direction_plot_r, aes(x = mean_log2fc_stim_vs_ctrl, y = gene, fill = direction_color)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey80") +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("higher in stimulation" = "#E76F51", "lower in stimulation" = "#2B8CBE"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Direction of top pattern genes",
    x = "Mean log2 fold-change: IFN-beta vs control",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
gene_direction_plot = top_gene_direction.sort_values("rank", ascending=False)
direction_colors = gene_direction_plot["direction"].map(
    {"up_in_stim": "#E76F51", "down_in_stim": "#2B8CBE"}
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.6))
ax.axvline(0, color="0.8")
ax.barh(
    gene_direction_plot["gene"],
    gene_direction_plot["mean_log2fc_stim_vs_ctrl"],
    color=direction_colors,
)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean log2 fold-change: IFN-beta vs control")
ax.set_ylabel("")
ax.set_title("Direction of top pattern genes")
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Most top genes for the implementation-specific IFN-associated pattern are higher in IFN-beta-stimulated cells. The top list includes canonical interferon-stimulated genes such as ISG15, ISG20, IFI6, IFIT3, IFIT1, MX1, IFIT2, IRF7, OAS1, PLSCR1, and BST2. The main exception among the top genes is FTH1, which has a high pattern weight but is lower in stimulation in this targeted summary. That exception is useful: it reminds you not to translate “top pattern gene” into “up-regulated gene” without checking directionality.

Compare Directionality For An Identity-Linked Pattern

The IFN-associated pattern is not the only pattern worth visualizing. Some patterns are more closely tied to than to stimulation. For those patterns, a stimulation-versus-control contrast is not always the most informative first direction check.

The next figure uses a dendritic / antigen-presentation-linked pattern as a teaching contrast. In the selected R run, this is Pattern3. In the saved Python-compatible output, the corresponding dendritic / antigen-presentation-linked pattern is Pattern6. The exact number changes across implementations, but the interpretation question is the same: do the top genes mark a PBMC identity, a stimulation response, or both?

To answer that, the figure uses two expression contrasts. The middle panel asks whether top genes are higher in the dominant annotated cell identity than in other PBMC identities. The right panel asks whether those same genes are higher after IFN-beta stimulation. That comparison keeps separate from and also keeps cell identity separate from condition.

The code below builds the same type of figure from the implementation-specific source table. In R, pivot_longer() turns two contrast columns into one plotting column so facet_wrap() can place the contrasts side by side. In Python, plt.subplots() creates the two side-by-side axes and a short loop draws one bar chart per contrast. Both versions practice the same programming idea: reshape the data so that the contrast you want to compare becomes a plotting variable.

  • R
  • Python
identity_pattern_label_r <- unique(identity_gene_direction_r$pattern)
dominant_identity_r <- unique(identity_gene_direction_r$dominant_cell_type)

identity_direction_long_r <- identity_gene_direction_r |>
  dplyr::arrange(desc(rank)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gene = factor(gene, levels = gene)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(identity_log2fc_dominant_vs_other, stim_log2fc_stim_vs_ctrl),
    names_to = "contrast",
    values_to = "mean_log2fc"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    contrast = dplyr::recode(
      contrast,
      identity_log2fc_dominant_vs_other = paste0(dominant_identity_r, " vs other PBMCs"),
      stim_log2fc_stim_vs_ctrl = "IFN-beta vs control"
    ),
    direction_label = dplyr::case_when(
      contrast == paste0(dominant_identity_r, " vs other PBMCs") & mean_log2fc >= 0 ~ paste0("higher in ", dominant_identity_r),
      contrast == paste0(dominant_identity_r, " vs other PBMCs") & mean_log2fc < 0 ~ "higher in other PBMCs",
      contrast == "IFN-beta vs control" & mean_log2fc >= 0 ~ "higher in stimulation",
      TRUE ~ "higher in control"
    )
  )

identity_direction_colors_r <- c("#168477", "#7E68B1", "#E76F51", "#2B8CBE")
names(identity_direction_colors_r) <- c(
  paste0("higher in ", dominant_identity_r),
  "higher in other PBMCs",
  "higher in stimulation",
  "higher in control"
)

ggplot(identity_direction_long_r, aes(x = mean_log2fc, y = gene, fill = direction_label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey80") +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ contrast, ncol = 2, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = identity_direction_colors_r,
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(identity_pattern_label_r, ": direction checks for an identity-linked pattern"),
    x = "Mean log2 fold-change",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
identity_direction_plot = identity_gene_direction.sort_values("rank", ascending=False).copy()
identity_pattern_label = identity_direction_plot["pattern"].iloc[0]
dominant_identity = identity_direction_plot["dominant_cell_type"].iloc[0]

plot_specs = [
    (
        f"{dominant_identity} vs other PBMCs",
        "identity_log2fc_dominant_vs_other",
        "#168477",
        "#7E68B1",
    ),
    (
        "IFN-beta vs control",
        "stim_log2fc_stim_vs_ctrl",
        "#E76F51",
        "#2B8CBE",
    ),
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(ncols=2, figsize=(9, 5.6), sharey=True)
y_positions = np.arange(len(identity_direction_plot))

for ax, (title, value_column, positive_color, negative_color) in zip(axes, plot_specs):
    values = identity_direction_plot[value_column]
    colors = np.where(values >= 0, positive_color, negative_color)
    ax.axvline(0, color="0.8")
    ax.barh(y_positions, values, color=colors)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("Mean log2 fold-change")
    ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)

axes[0].set_yticks(y_positions)
axes[0].set_yticklabels(identity_direction_plot["gene"])
axes[0].set_ylabel("")
fig.suptitle(f"{identity_pattern_label}: direction checks for an identity-linked pattern")
legend_handles = [
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], color="#168477", lw=8, label=f"higher in {dominant_identity}"),
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], color="#7E68B1", lw=8, label="higher in other PBMCs"),
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], color="#E76F51", lw=8, label="higher in stimulation"),
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], color="#2B8CBE", lw=8, label="higher in control"),
]
fig.legend(handles=legend_handles, loc="lower center", ncol=2, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.1, 1, 0.96])
plt.show()

The identity-linked direction check changes the interpretation. The top genes for this pattern are not mainly canonical IFN-response genes. They include CD74 and several HLA genes, which are consistent with antigen presentation and dendritic-cell-linked structure. Those genes are higher in dendritic cells than in other PBMC identities, while most are not higher after IFN-beta stimulation in this summary. That is exactly why this second direction check matters: a meaningful CoGAPS pattern does not have to be a stimulation-response pattern.

Visualization Checkpoint

By the end of this section, you should be able to read the selected-model visual evidence as a set of linked checks:

  • The pattern screen identifies the strongest stimulation-associated candidate in each saved implementation.
  • The paired donor plot checks whether the stimulation shift appears across matched donor aliquots.
  • The cell-type plot asks whether the same pattern is broad across PBMC identities.
  • The heatmap shows that other patterns have different condition and cell-type behavior.
  • The gene-direction plot connects top CoGAPS genes to whether those genes rise or fall after IFN-beta stimulation.
  • The identity-linked direction plot shows that some top genes mark an immune-cell identity rather than a stimulation response.

The next section moves from visual inspection to model interpretation. You will inspect the same CoGAPS outputs more directly, identify the IFN-associated pattern from the saved metrics and pattern tables, and connect activity, top genes, and directionality into a cautious biological interpretation.

Data Analysis

You have now imported the prepared PBMC data, inspected model-selection evidence, and visualized CoGAPS in relation to cell identity, IFN-beta stimulation, and gene direction. This section turns those pieces into an evidence chain: first check that the selected model is suitable to interpret, then use the four main questions to organize the biological interpretation.

The key habit is to avoid naming a pattern from one clue alone. A CoGAPS pattern has two linked parts: and . A pattern can have high-weight interferon-stimulated genes, but the cells also need to show activity where an interferon response is expected. A gene can have a high CoGAPS weight, but that weight does not by itself tell you whether the gene is higher or lower after IFN-beta stimulation.

The selected R model is the primary model you will interpret. The Python tab lets you repeat the same checks with saved Python outputs. Because pattern numbers can differ across runs, the phrase “” is usually safer than a numbered label. When this section discusses a specific saved run, it states the run-specific label explicitly.

Questions answered in this section

  1. What latent transcriptional programs are present in IFN-beta-stimulated and control PBMC single-cell RNA-seq data?
  2. Can CoGAPS help distinguish broad stimulation-associated activity from cell-type-linked immune programs?
  3. Which genes define the strongest IFN-associated pattern, and what is their direction in stimulation?
  4. How does the IFN-associated pattern vary across annotated PBMC cell types?

Load The Analysis Tables

The selected-model files are lightweight tables exported from the saved CoGAPS runs. They let the case study inspect model evidence without requiring every learner to load a full model object. In this first step, the code reads the tables that later chunks reuse.

In R, readr::read_csv() reads comma-separated tables and readr::read_tsv() reads tab-separated pattern matrices. The pipe operator |> passes the result of one step into the next step, which makes the code read from left to right. In Python, pandas.read_csv() plays the same role, and Path objects keep file paths explicit.

The R run labels the IFN-associated pattern as Pattern4. The Python-compatible output labels the corresponding signal as Pattern5. That difference is not a contradiction. CoGAPS pattern numbers are labels assigned inside a run; they are not stable biological names.

Carry-Forward Check: Is The Selected Model Appropriate To Interpret?

Before interpreting a latent pattern, ask whether the model run looks stable enough to support interpretation. CoGAPS is a matrix-factorization method, not a simple optimizer that must make the smaller at every printed step. Some movement during sampling is expected. What you want to see is a large early improvement followed by a much flatter region where the trace changes only modestly.

The below comes from the selected R run because the R implementation is the primary model for this case study and has the richest saved diagnostic record. The dashed line marks the transition between and the . Equilibration is the burn-in-like phase in which the sampler moves away from its starting state. Sampling is the phase used to summarize the final pattern matrices.

How to use this model-check section

  • R analysis path: run these diagnostic chunks. They use saved trace, snapshot, and uncertainty files from the selected R CoGAPS model.
  • Python analysis path: read the rendered diagnostic evidence here, then continue with the Python tabs in Question 1. These particular diagnostics are shown from R because the selected R run is the primary model and has the richest saved diagnostic record.
  • Full reproduction path: use the Full Reproduction Guide if you want to rerun the selected model and regenerate these diagnostic files yourself.

The first plotting chunk builds the chi-square trace in two steps. It first adds a phase column so each printed iteration is labeled as either equilibration or sampling. Then ggplot() draws the trace as a connected line, adds colored points for the two phases, and places a dashed vertical line at relative progress 0.5, where sampling begins.

trace_plot_r <- trace_r |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    phase = dplyr::if_else(relative_progress <= 0.5, "equilibration", "sampling")
  )

ggplot(trace_plot_r, aes(x = relative_progress, y = chisq)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2F5D8C", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(color = phase), size = 2.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "#102A43") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("equilibration" = "#E76F51", "sampling" = "#2A9D8F")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(
    title = "Selected R model reaches a chi-square plateau",
    subtitle = "Relative progress 0.5 marks the end of equilibration and the start of sampling.",
    x = "Relative progress through the full run",
    y = "Chi-square",
    color = "Phase"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The plot supports using the model, but it should not be oversold. The trace still has small stochastic changes late in the run. That is normal for a sampler. The important point is that the large early changes have mostly settled before the final summaries are interpreted.

Snapshots give a second stability check. A snapshot is a saved view of the model state during the run. The code below focuses on the gene-loading matrix, because top genes are central to biological interpretation. The column mean_top_overlap asks whether the top genes in each snapshot resemble the top genes in the final summary.

The plotting code filters the snapshot table to matrix A, the gene-weight matrix, because this check is about top-gene stability. It then orders snapshots by phase, draws mean_top_overlap over time, and adds a dotted reference line at 0.9. Values near the top of the plot mean the snapshot top genes are very similar to the final top genes.

snapshot_a_r <- snapshot_summary_r |>
  dplyr::filter(matrix == "A", !is.na(mean_top_overlap)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    phase = factor(phase, levels = c("equilibration", "sampling"))
  )

ggplot(snapshot_a_r, aes(x = snapshot_label, y = mean_top_overlap, color = phase)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.9, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey45") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("equilibration" = "#E76F51", "sampling" = "#2A9D8F")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  labs(
    title = "Top genes stabilize before the final summary",
    subtitle = "Higher overlap means the snapshot top genes resemble the final top genes.",
    x = "Iteration within phase",
    y = "Mean top-gene overlap",
    color = "Phase"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

A third diagnostic looks at . The table below is not a pass/fail test. It helps you notice which patterns have more variability in their gene weights or cell activities. The IFN-associated pattern has a strong biological signal and interpretable top genes, but its uncertainty is still worth carrying forward as part of the evidence.

Two columns matter most here. Mean cell-activity SD summarizes the average posterior standard deviation of the pattern’s cell activity scores. A larger value means that, across cells, the model sampled a wider range of plausible activity values for that pattern. Median top-gene loading CV summarizes uncertainty in the gene weights for the pattern’s strongest genes; the compares uncertainty with the size of the estimated loading, and the median keeps one unusually noisy top gene from dominating the summary.

These statistics are uncertainty summaries, not biological effect sizes. A high cell-activity SD does not mean the pattern is more biologically important, and a lower loading CV does not by itself name the pattern. Instead, use them beside the trace, snapshot stability, top genes, and stimulation/cell-type evidence.

The table marks the run-specific IFN-associated pattern, then shows the two uncertainty summaries beside the other selected-model patterns. First find the IFN-associated row, then compare its uncertainty values with the rest of the model.

uncertainty_display_r <- uncertainty_summary_r |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    pattern_role = dplyr::if_else(
      pattern == ifn_pattern_r,
      "IFN-associated pattern in selected R run",
      "other selected-model pattern"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    pattern,
    pattern_role,
    mean_factor_sd,
    top_gene_median_loading_cv
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    mean_factor_sd = round(mean_factor_sd, 4),
    top_gene_median_loading_cv = round(top_gene_median_loading_cv, 4)
  )

knitr::kable(
  uncertainty_display_r,
  col.names = c(
    "Pattern",
    "Role in this run",
    "Mean cell-activity SD",
    "Median top-gene loading CV"
  )
)
Pattern Role in this run Mean cell-activity SD Median top-gene loading CV
Pattern1 other selected-model pattern 0.0042 0.0119
Pattern2 other selected-model pattern 0.0044 0.0115
Pattern3 other selected-model pattern 0.0044 0.0160
Pattern4 IFN-associated pattern in selected R run 0.0105 0.0233
Pattern5 other selected-model pattern 0.0028 0.0105
Pattern6 other selected-model pattern 0.0148 0.0229

In this run, the IFN-associated pattern is Pattern4. Its mean cell-activity SD is 0.0105, which is higher than several other patterns but lower than Pattern6. Its median top-gene loading CV is 0.0233, similar to Pattern6 and higher than the other rows. That means the IFN-associated pattern is not the least uncertain pattern in the model, so you should not interpret a single cell’s exact activity score too literally. The more important question is whether the same pattern is supported by several kinds of evidence. Here, the uncertainty table does not stand alone: it is read beside the chi-square trace, the snapshot top-gene stability check, the IFN-linked top genes, and the paired donor activity results below.

Together, the trace, snapshot, and uncertainty summaries support proceeding with interpretation. They do not prove that this is the only possible model. They show that the selected R run behaved coherently enough for the focused biological questions in this case study.

Question 1: What Latent Transcriptional Programs Are Present?

This question asks what kinds of signals the selected CoGAPS model learned from IFN-beta-stimulated and control PBMC single-cell RNA-seq data. You begin by comparing patterns by evidence, not by numbered labels. Then you make a working inventory of candidate programs using stimulation association, top genes, cell-type activity, and gene direction.

Match Patterns By Evidence, Not By Number

The R and Python-compatible outputs should not be compared by pattern number. Instead, compare what each pattern does. The code below matches patterns using two pieces of evidence:

  • : do the two patterns assign high activity to the same cells?
  • : do the two patterns use similar top genes?

The programming move here is a pairwise comparison. The code creates every R-pattern by Python-pattern pair, computes a similarity score for each pair, and then chooses non-overlapping best matches. In R, expand.grid() creates all pattern pairs. In Python, nested for loops do the same job in a way that is easy to read.

  • R
  • Python
python_matrices_r <- load_lightweight_pattern_matrices_r(
  file.path(SELECTED_PYTHON_RESULTS_DIR_R, "pattern_gene_weights.tsv.gz"),
  file.path(SELECTED_PYTHON_RESULTS_DIR_R, "pattern_cell_activities.tsv.gz")
)

A_python_for_match_r <- python_matrices_r$A
P_python_for_match_r <- python_matrices_r$P

common_cells_r <- intersect(rownames(P_r), rownames(P_python_for_match_r))
common_genes_r <- intersect(rownames(A_r), rownames(A_python_for_match_r))

pair_grid_r <- expand.grid(
  r_pattern = pattern_columns_r(colnames(P_r)),
  python_pattern = pattern_columns_r(colnames(P_python_for_match_r)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

top_n_match_r <- 50L
pair_grid_r$activity_spearman <- NA_real_
pair_grid_r$top50_overlap <- NA_integer_
pair_grid_r$top50_jaccard <- NA_real_

for (i in seq_len(nrow(pair_grid_r))) {
  r_pat <- pair_grid_r$r_pattern[i]
  py_pat <- pair_grid_r$python_pattern[i]

  pair_grid_r$activity_spearman[i] <- suppressWarnings(cor(
    P_r[common_cells_r, r_pat],
    P_python_for_match_r[common_cells_r, py_pat],
    method = "spearman"
  ))

  r_weights_i <- A_r[common_genes_r, r_pat]
  names(r_weights_i) <- common_genes_r
  py_weights_i <- A_python_for_match_r[common_genes_r, py_pat]
  names(py_weights_i) <- common_genes_r
  r_top <- names(sort(r_weights_i, decreasing = TRUE))[seq_len(top_n_match_r)]
  py_top <- names(sort(py_weights_i, decreasing = TRUE))[seq_len(top_n_match_r)]
  pair_grid_r$top50_overlap[i] <- length(intersect(r_top, py_top))
  pair_grid_r$top50_jaccard[i] <- length(intersect(r_top, py_top)) / length(union(r_top, py_top))
}

greedy_order_r <- pair_grid_r |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(activity_spearman), dplyr::desc(top50_jaccard))

matched_rows_r <- list()
used_r_patterns <- character()
used_python_patterns <- character()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(greedy_order_r))) {
  row_i <- greedy_order_r[i, ]
  if (!(row_i$r_pattern %in% used_r_patterns) &&
      !(row_i$python_pattern %in% used_python_patterns)) {
    matched_rows_r[[length(matched_rows_r) + 1L]] <- row_i
    used_r_patterns <- c(used_r_patterns, row_i$r_pattern)
    used_python_patterns <- c(used_python_patterns, row_i$python_pattern)
  }
}

  dplyr::arrange(as.integer(sub("Pattern", "", r_pattern))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    activity_spearman = round(activity_spearman, 3),
    top50_jaccard = round(top50_jaccard, 3)
  )

r_weights = pd.read_csv(R_PATTERN_GENE_WEIGHTS_TSV_GZ, sep="\t").set_index("gene")
r_activities = pd.read_csv(R_PATTERN_CELL_ACTIVITIES_TSV_GZ, sep="\t").set_index("cell_barcode")
r_weights.columns = [col.replace("Pattern_", "Pattern") for col in r_weights.columns]
r_activities.columns = [col.replace("Pattern_", "Pattern") for col in r_activities.columns]

common_cells = r_activities.index.intersection(P_py.index)
common_genes = r_weights.index.intersection(A_py.index)

def top_gene_set(weight_table, pattern, n=50):
    return set(weight_table.loc[common_genes, pattern].sort_values(ascending=False).head(n).index)

pair_records = []
for r_pattern in pattern_columns(r_weights):
    for python_pattern in pattern_columns(A_py):
        r_activity = r_activities.loc[common_cells, r_pattern].rank()
        python_activity = P_py.loc[common_cells, python_pattern].rank()
        activity_spearman = r_activity.corr(python_activity)

        r_top = top_gene_set(r_weights, r_pattern)
        python_top = top_gene_set(A_py, python_pattern)
        overlap = len(r_top.intersection(python_top))
        jaccard = overlap / len(r_top.union(python_top))

        pair_records.append(
            {
                "R pattern": r_pattern,
                "Python-compatible pattern": python_pattern,
                "Cell-activity Spearman": activity_spearman,
                "Top-50 gene overlap": overlap,
                "Top-50 Jaccard": jaccard,
            }
        )

pair_table = pd.DataFrame(pair_records).sort_values(
    ["Cell-activity Spearman", "Top-50 Jaccard"],
    ascending=False,
)

used_r = set()
used_python = set()
matched_records = []
for _, row in pair_table.iterrows():
    if row["R pattern"] not in used_r and row["Python-compatible pattern"] not in used_python:
        matched_records.append(row)
        used_r.add(row["R pattern"])
        used_python.add(row["Python-compatible pattern"])

matched_patterns = (
    pd.DataFrame(matched_records)
    .sort_values("R pattern", key=lambda s: s.str.replace("Pattern", "").astype(int))
    .round({"Cell-activity Spearman": 3, "Top-50 Jaccard": 3})
)

The matched table shows that the R and Python-compatible outputs recover the same major pattern structure, even though the pattern numbers are permuted. In particular, the selected R IFN-associated pattern, Pattern4, matches the Python-compatible IFN-associated pattern, Pattern5, with very high cell-activity agreement and complete top-50 gene overlap. That agreement gives you a useful check on interpretation: the main biological signal is not tied to one implementation-specific pattern number.

Summarize The Candidate Programs

Now that you know not to rely on pattern numbers alone, you can ask what kinds of are present. This table is a working inventory, not a final naming ceremony. It combines four clues that you have already seen in earlier sections:

  • stimulation association: whether pattern activity tracks IFN-beta stimulation,
  • dominant cell-type activity: where the pattern is strongest on average,
  • top genes: which genes have the largest CoGAPS weights,
  • direction among top genes: whether those top genes tend to be higher or lower after stimulation.

The code below uses simple, visible rules to assign cautious working interpretations. For example, a pattern with high stimulation correlation and interferon-stimulated genes is marked as IFN-associated. A pattern with CD74 and HLA genes is marked as antigen-presentation-linked. A pattern with monocyte markers and highest mean activity in monocytes is treated as monocyte-linked. These labels are starting points for interpretation, not labels that CoGAPS knew in advance.

As you read the code, focus on the data-wrangling pattern rather than trying to memorize every function name. Both tabs do the same four jobs:

  1. Start from one row per CoGAPS pattern. The source table already contains pattern-level summaries, such as stimulation correlation, mean activity in control and stimulated cells, the dominant cell type, and the top genes.
  2. Add the directionality summary. The code joins in the count of top genes that are higher or lower after IFN-beta stimulation, so the final table can keep CoGAPS weights and expression direction side by side.
  3. Create readable evidence columns. The code calculates stim - control, keeps only the first few top genes for display, and turns several numeric columns into short phrases that are easier to scan.
  4. Apply cautious interpretation rules. The rules use the evidence already in the table. They do not rerun CoGAPS, and they do not replace biological judgment.

In R, the pipe operator |> reads as “then.” The code starts with pattern_summary_r, then uses left_join() to add direction counts, mutate() to create new columns, case_when() to assign the working interpretation, arrange() to put Pattern1 through Pattern6 in order, and select() to keep only the columns shown in the table. In Python, the same idea appears as a method chain: merge() adds the direction counts, assign() creates new columns, apply() runs the interpretation function once per row, sort_values() orders the patterns, and the final column selection keeps the output focused.

  • R
  • Python
first_genes_r <- function(gene_text, n = 4L) {
  vapply(
    strsplit(gene_text, ",\\s*"),
    function(genes) paste(head(genes, n), collapse = ", "),
    character(1)
  )
}

program_inventory_r <- pattern_summary_r |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    direction_summary_r |>
      dplyr::select(pattern, n_up_in_stim, n_down_in_stim),
    by = "pattern"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    activity_shift = mean_activity_stim - mean_activity_ctrl,
    top_genes_top4 = first_genes_r(top_genes_top15),
    working_interpretation = dplyr::case_when(
      corr_with_stim >= 0.70 &
        grepl("ISG15|IFIT|MX1|OAS1|IRF7", top_genes_top15) ~
        "Broad IFN-associated stimulation",
      corr_with_stim >= 0.20 &
        grepl("CXCL10|APOBEC3A|RSAD2|ISG15", top_genes_top15) ~
        "Monocyte-biased stimulation-linked",
      grepl("CD74|HLA-DRA|HLA-DRB1|HLA-DPA1|HLA-DPB1", top_genes_top15) ~
        "Dendritic / antigen-presentation-linked",
      dominant_cell_type == "FCGR3A+ Monocytes" ~
        "FCGR3A+ monocyte-linked",
      dominant_cell_type == "CD14+ Monocytes" ~
        "CD14+ monocyte-linked baseline",
      dominant_cell_type == "CD4 T cells" ~
        "T-cell / lymphocyte-linked baseline",
      TRUE ~ "additional immune-cell-linked signal"
    ),
    stimulation_evidence = paste0(
      "corr = ", round(corr_with_stim, 2),
      "; stim - control = ", round(activity_shift, 2)
    ),
    identity_gene_evidence = paste0(
      "highest in ", dominant_cell_type,
      "; top genes: ", top_genes_top4
    ),
    direction_evidence = paste0(
      n_up_in_stim, " up / ",
      n_down_in_stim, " down among top 15 genes"
    ),
    pattern_index = as.integer(sub("Pattern", "", pattern))
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(pattern_index) |>
  dplyr::select(
    pattern,
    working_interpretation,
    stimulation_evidence,
    identity_gene_evidence,
    direction_evidence
  )

)

def first_genes(gene_text, n=4):
    genes = [gene.strip() for gene in str(gene_text).split(",")]
    return ", ".join(genes[:n])

def interpret_program(row):
    genes = str(row["top_genes_top15"])
    dominant = row["dominant_cell_type"]
    corr = row["corr_with_stim"]

    if corr >= 0.70 and any(gene in genes for gene in ["ISG15", "IFIT", "MX1", "OAS1", "IRF7"]):
        return "Broad IFN-associated stimulation"
    if corr >= 0.20 and any(gene in genes for gene in ["CXCL10", "APOBEC3A", "RSAD2", "ISG15"]):
        return "Monocyte-biased stimulation-linked"
    if any(gene in genes for gene in ["CD74", "HLA-DRA", "HLA-DRB1", "HLA-DPA1", "HLA-DPB1"]):
        return "Dendritic / antigen-presentation-linked"
    if dominant == "FCGR3A+ Monocytes":
        return "FCGR3A+ monocyte-linked"
    if dominant == "CD14+ Monocytes":
        return "CD14+ monocyte-linked baseline"
    if dominant == "CD4 T cells":
        return "T-cell / lymphocyte-linked baseline"
    return "additional immune-cell-linked signal"

program_inventory = (
    pattern_summary
    .merge(
        direction_summary[
            ["pattern", "n_up_in_stim", "n_down_in_stim"]
        ],
        on="pattern",
        how="left",
    )
    .assign(
        activity_shift=lambda df: df["mean_activity_stim"] - df["mean_activity_ctrl"],
        top_genes_top4=lambda df: df["top_genes_top15"].apply(first_genes),
    )
)

program_inventory["Working interpretation"] = program_inventory.apply(interpret_program, axis=1)
program_inventory["Stimulation evidence"] = (
    "corr = " + program_inventory["corr_with_stim"].round(2).astype(str)
    + "; stim - control = " + program_inventory["activity_shift"].round(2).astype(str)
)
program_inventory["Identity / gene evidence"] = (
    "highest in " + program_inventory["dominant_cell_type"]
    + "; top genes: " + program_inventory["top_genes_top4"]
)
program_inventory["Direction check"] = (
    program_inventory["n_up_in_stim"].astype(int).astype(str)
    + " up / "
    + program_inventory["n_down_in_stim"].astype(int).astype(str)
    + " down among top 15 genes"
)

program_inventory_display = (
    program_inventory
    .assign(pattern_index=lambda df: df["pattern"].str.replace("Pattern", "").astype(int))
    .sort_values("pattern_index")
    [["pattern", "Working interpretation", "Stimulation evidence", "Identity / gene evidence", "Direction check"]]
    .rename(columns={"pattern": "Pattern"})
)

print(render_table(program_inventory_display))

Check The Evidence Behind The Working Labels

The working interpretations above should not be read as automatic names. They are short labels for evidence patterns. A label is strongest when two kinds of evidence agree:

  • local model evidence, such as stimulation correlation, dominant cell-type activity, top genes, and expression direction; and
  • prior biological knowledge, such as known interferon-stimulated genes, antigen-presentation genes, or immune-cell annotations from the source study.

This distinction matters because not all six labels have the same strength. Some are gene-anchored: the top genes have a well-established biological role. Others are more activity-anchored: the pattern is strongest in a particular annotated cell population, but the top genes are not enough by themselves to name a pathway.

  • Pattern4, broad IFN-associated stimulation, has the strongest support. It has high stimulation correlation, a large positive stimulated-minus-control activity shift, mostly up-regulated top genes, and top genes such as ISG15, ISG20, IFI6, IFIT3, IFIT1, MX1, OAS1, and IRF7. Those genes are consistent with the IFN-beta perturbation in the source study and with the interferon-stimulated gene biology introduced in the Context section (Kang et al. 2018; Chyuan, Tzeng, and Chen 2019; Catalina et al. 2019).

  • Pattern5, monocyte-biased stimulation-linked, has a moderate positive stimulation association and many stimulation-up genes, including interferon-related genes. Its “monocyte-biased” part comes from the local activity evidence: the pattern is strongest in annotated CD14+ monocytes. That is why the label is more cautious than Pattern4. It suggests an IFN-responsive signal with stronger monocyte activity, not a fully separate monocyte pathway.

  • Pattern3, dendritic / antigen-presentation-linked, is strongly supported by its top genes. CD74 and HLA class II genes such as HLA-DRA, HLA-DRB1, HLA-DPA1, and HLA-DPB1 are tied to MHC class II antigen processing and presentation (Blum, Wearsch, and Cresswell 2013). The local activity evidence adds that this pattern is strongest in annotated dendritic cells, a blood immune-cell population where antigen-presentation biology is expected (Villani et al. 2017).

  • Pattern1 and Pattern2, monocyte-linked, are mainly activity-anchored. Pattern1 is strongest in annotated FCGR3A+ monocytes and includes FCGR3A among its top genes. Pattern2 is strongest in annotated CD14+ monocytes, but its top genes include several broad baseline or stress-response genes, such as ferritin genes. Human blood monocytes are often discussed using CD14/CD16-related distinctions, and single-cell blood atlases show that monocyte and dendritic-cell annotations can contain multiple related subtypes (Ziegler-Heitbrock et al. 2010; Villani et al. 2017). In this table, those labels should therefore be read as “where the pattern is strongest,” not as complete pathway names.

  • Pattern6, T-cell / lymphocyte-linked baseline, is also activity-anchored. It is strongest in annotated CD4 T cells and has lower activity after stimulation, but its top genes are not a clean T-cell receptor or cytokine pathway. The safest interpretation is that this pattern marks lymphocyte-neighborhood baseline structure in this run. This is still useful, because a latent model can contain both cell-identity-like signals and cell-activity-like signals in the same dataset (Kotliar et al. 2019).

Taken together, the selected model does not recover only one stimulation signal. It contains a strongly supported IFN-associated stimulation pattern, a second more cautious monocyte-biased stimulation-linked pattern, a gene-anchored antigen-presentation-linked pattern, and several activity-anchored immune-cell-linked baseline patterns. The next questions test the most important part of that inventory more deeply: whether the IFN-associated pattern behaves like a broad stimulation response rather than a mislabeled cell-type pattern.

Question 2: Can CoGAPS Separate Stimulation From Cell-Type-Linked Structure?

This question asks whether the selected model contains a broad IFN-beta stimulation signal while still retaining immune-cell-linked structure. You answer it by testing the paired stimulation shift, comparing the IFN-associated pattern with a simple interferon-stimulated gene score, and contrasting that pattern with an antigen-presentation-linked pattern.

Here, compare means asking whether two different kinds of evidence point to the same biological signal. If the IFN-associated CoGAPS pattern rises after stimulation and also agrees with a simple interferon-stimulated gene score, that supports interpreting the pattern as an IFN-beta response rather than as a numerical pattern with no clear biology.

Here, contrast means setting that IFN-associated pattern beside a different pattern that should behave differently. An -linked pattern, for example, may be defined by CD74 and HLA class II genes rather than by a broad stimulation shift. Seeing those differences helps you separate a shared treatment-response signal from immune-cell-linked biology (Blum, Wearsch, and Cresswell 2013).

Test The Paired IFN Activity Shift

The source experiment used a : each donor contributed a control aliquot and an IFN-beta-stimulated aliquot. That design is valuable because each donor can serve as their own comparison. Instead of asking only whether all stimulated cells have higher activity on average, you can ask whether the shift appears within each matched donor pair.

The code below filters to the IFN-associated pattern, separates control and stimulated mean activity by donor, computes stim - control, and then performs a one-sided . The sign test asks a simple question: if stimulation had no consistent direction, how surprising would it be to see this many donor pairs shift upward?

  • R
  • Python
ifn_replicate_r <- activity_by_replicate_r |>
  dplyr::filter(pattern == ifn_pattern_r)

ctrl_replicate_r <- ifn_replicate_r |>
  dplyr::filter(condition == "ctrl") |>
  dplyr::select(replicate, ctrl_mean_activity = mean_activity, ctrl_n_cells = n_cells)

stim_replicate_r <- ifn_replicate_r |>
  dplyr::filter(condition == "stim") |>
  dplyr::select(replicate, stim_mean_activity = mean_activity, stim_n_cells = n_cells)

ifn_pair_shift_r <- dplyr::inner_join(
  ctrl_replicate_r,
  stim_replicate_r,
  by = "replicate"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(activity_shift = stim_mean_activity - ctrl_mean_activity)

n_positive_r <- sum(ifn_pair_shift_r$activity_shift > 0)
n_nonzero_r <- sum(ifn_pair_shift_r$activity_shift != 0)
sign_test_r <- binom.test(
  n_positive_r,
  n_nonzero_r,
  p = 0.5,
  alternative = "greater"
)

paired_shift_summary_r <- tibble::tibble(
  `IFN-associated pattern` = ifn_pattern_r,
  `matched donor pairs` = nrow(ifn_pair_shift_r),
  `pairs higher after stimulation` = n_positive_r,
  `mean shift` = round(mean(ifn_pair_shift_r$activity_shift), 3),
  `median shift` = round(median(ifn_pair_shift_r$activity_shift), 3),
  `one-sided sign-test p-value` = signif(sign_test_r$p.value, 3)
)

knitr::kable(paired_shift_summary_r)
IFN-associated pattern matched donor pairs pairs higher after stimulation mean shift median shift one-sided sign-test p-value
Pattern4 8 8 0.281 0.283 0.00391 
from math import comb

def one_sided_sign_test_pvalue(n_positive, n_nonzero):
    """Exact one-sided sign-test probability under a 50/50 null."""
    return sum(comb(n_nonzero, k) for k in range(n_positive, n_nonzero + 1)) / (2 ** n_nonzero)

ifn_replicate = activity_by_replicate.loc[
    activity_by_replicate["pattern"] == ifn_pattern_py
]

ifn_pair_shift = (
    ifn_replicate.pivot_table(
        index="replicate",
        columns="condition",
        values="mean_activity"
    )
    .dropna()
    .reset_index()
)
ifn_pair_shift["activity_shift"] = ifn_pair_shift["stim"] - ifn_pair_shift["ctrl"]

n_positive = int((ifn_pair_shift["activity_shift"] > 0).sum())
n_nonzero = int((ifn_pair_shift["activity_shift"] != 0).sum())
sign_pvalue = one_sided_sign_test_pvalue(n_positive, n_nonzero)

paired_shift_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "IFN-associated pattern": [ifn_pattern_py],
        "matched donor pairs": [len(ifn_pair_shift)],
        "pairs higher after stimulation": [n_positive],
        "mean shift": [round(ifn_pair_shift["activity_shift"].mean(), 3)],
        "median shift": [round(ifn_pair_shift["activity_shift"].median(), 3)],
        "one-sided sign-test p-value": [f"{sign_pvalue:.3g}"],
    }
)

print(render_table(paired_shift_summary))
IFN-associated pattern matched donor pairs pairs higher after stimulation mean shift median shift one-sided sign-test p-value
Pattern5 8 8 0.281 0.283 0.00391

Read the table as a donor-paired direction check, not as a cell-level test. Each donor contributes one matched comparison: the mean IFN-associated pattern activity in that donor’s stimulated aliquot minus the mean activity in that donor’s control aliquot.

  • IFN-associated pattern gives the run-specific pattern label being tested. In the selected R run, this is Pattern4; in another run, the same biological signal can have a different pattern number.
  • Matched donor pairs is the number of donors that have both a control and stimulated measurement available for this comparison.
  • Pairs higher after stimulation counts how many donor pairs have a positive stim - control shift. Here, 8 means every matched donor pair moved in the same upward direction.
  • Mean shift and median shift summarize the size of the donor-level activity change. The mean is the average shift across donors; the median is the middle donor shift and is less sensitive to one unusually large or small donor response.
  • One-sided sign-test p-value asks how surprising it would be to observe at least this many upward shifts if upward and downward shifts were equally likely. With 8 of 8 donor pairs higher after stimulation, the probability under that no-direction null is 0.00391, or about 0.4%.

The p-value comes from the directions of the paired shifts, not from thousands of individual cells and not from the size of the shifts. That is why the table reports both pieces of evidence: the sign test checks whether the direction is consistent across donors, while the mean and median shifts show how large the activity change is on the CoGAPS activity scale.

For the selected R run, all eight matched donor pairs have higher IFN-associated activity after stimulation. The Python-compatible output shows the same qualitative result for its matched IFN-associated pattern. This is stronger evidence than a pooled cell-level average because it respects the paired study design.

The sign test is intentionally modest. It does not claim that IFN-beta stimulation has the same effect size in every donor, and it does not replace a full clinical model. It simply checks whether the direction of the pattern activity shift is consistent across the donor pairs in this dataset.

Optional Formal Check: Account For Donor With A Mixed Model

The paired sign test checks whether the direction of change is consistent across donors. A asks a slightly different question: after allowing each donor to have their own baseline activity, is the average stimulation effect still positive?

This is useful because donors can differ before stimulation. One donor may have higher baseline pattern activity than another donor even before IFN-beta is added. If you ignore that pairing, the analysis can mix two ideas together: differences between donors and the effect of stimulation within the same donor.

The model below separates those ideas. It treats condition as the effect of interest: stimulated versus control. It treats donor as the grouping term: measurements from the same donor are related because they come from matched aliquots. In plain language, the model asks:

After accounting for each donor’s baseline activity level, how much higher is the IFN-associated pattern activity in stimulated aliquots than in control aliquots?

The model is fit to donor-level mean activity, not to every cell. In this dataset, that means each donor contributes one control mean and one stimulated mean for the IFN-associated pattern. This keeps the analysis aligned with the experimental design and avoids treating thousands of cells as thousands of independent donors.

The R and Python chunks below do the same analysis in parallel:

  1. They start from the donor-by-condition activity table for the IFN-associated pattern.
  2. They keep only the columns needed for the model: donor, condition, and mean activity.
  3. They make control the reference condition, so the stimulation coefficient is interpreted as stim - control.
  4. They fit a random-intercept mixed model. In R, nlme::lme(mean_activity ~ condition, random = ~ 1 | replicate) means “estimate the condition effect, while allowing each donor to have its own baseline.” In Python, statsmodels uses the same idea with mean_activity ~ condition_stim and groups = replicate.
  5. They extract the stimulation effect, its uncertainty, the p-value, and the variation left over after accounting for condition and donor.
  6. They place those quantities into a small summary table so the statistical result can be read beside the simpler paired sign-test result.
  • R
  • Python
mixed_model_data_r <- ifn_replicate_r |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("ctrl", "stim")),
    replicate = factor(replicate)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(replicate, condition, mean_activity)

ifn_mixed_model_r <- nlme::lme(
  mean_activity ~ condition,
  random = ~ 1 | replicate,
  data = mixed_model_data_r,
  method = "REML",
  control = nlme::lmeControl(msMaxIter = 100, opt = "optim")
)

mixed_coef_r <- summary(ifn_mixed_model_r)$tTable
mixed_condition_r <- mixed_coef_r["conditionstim", ]
mixed_varcorr_r <- nlme::VarCorr(ifn_mixed_model_r)

mixed_effect_r <- unname(mixed_condition_r["Value"])
mixed_pvalue_r <- unname(mixed_condition_r["p-value"])
mixed_donor_sd_r <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(mixed_varcorr_r["(Intercept)", "StdDev"]))
mixed_residual_sd_r <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(mixed_varcorr_r["Residual", "StdDev"]))

mixed_model_summary_r <- tibble::tibble(
  `IFN-associated pattern` = ifn_pattern_r,
  `model question` = "stimulated mean activity vs control, accounting for donor",
  `estimated stimulation effect` = round(mixed_effect_r, 3),
  `standard error` = round(unname(mixed_condition_r["Std.Error"]), 3),
  `t statistic` = round(unname(mixed_condition_r["t-value"]), 2),
  `p-value` = format.pval(mixed_pvalue_r, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
  `donor baseline SD` = round(mixed_donor_sd_r, 3),
  `residual SD` = round(mixed_residual_sd_r, 3)
)

knitr::kable(mixed_model_summary_r)
IFN-associated pattern model question estimated stimulation effect standard error t statistic p-value donor baseline SD residual SD
Pattern4 stimulated mean activity vs control, accounting for donor 0.281 0.006 46.13 <0.001 0 0.012 
import warnings
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

mixed_model_data = ifn_replicate[
    ["replicate", "condition", "mean_activity"]
].copy()
mixed_model_data["condition"] = pd.Categorical(
    mixed_model_data["condition"],
    categories=["ctrl", "stim"],
    ordered=True,
)
mixed_model_data["condition_stim"] = (
    mixed_model_data["condition"] == "stim"
).astype(int)

ifn_mixed_model = smf.mixedlm(
    "mean_activity ~ condition_stim",
    mixed_model_data,
    groups=mixed_model_data["replicate"],
)

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    try:
        ifn_mixed_result = ifn_mixed_model.fit(
            reml=True,
            method="lbfgs",
            disp=False,
        )
    except Exception:
        ifn_mixed_result = ifn_mixed_model.fit(
            reml=True,
            method="powell",
            maxiter=500,
            disp=False,
        )

mixed_effect = float(ifn_mixed_result.params["condition_stim"])
mixed_pvalue = float(ifn_mixed_result.pvalues["condition_stim"])
mixed_donor_sd = float(np.sqrt(ifn_mixed_result.cov_re.iloc[0, 0]))
mixed_residual_sd = float(np.sqrt(ifn_mixed_result.scale))

mixed_model_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "IFN-associated pattern": [ifn_pattern_py],
        "model question": [
            "stimulated mean activity vs control, accounting for donor"
        ],
        "estimated stimulation effect": [round(mixed_effect, 3)],
        "standard error": [round(float(ifn_mixed_result.bse["condition_stim"]), 3)],
        "z statistic": [round(float(ifn_mixed_result.tvalues["condition_stim"]), 2)],
        "p-value": ["<0.001" if mixed_pvalue < 0.001 else f"{mixed_pvalue:.3f}"],
        "donor baseline SD": [round(mixed_donor_sd, 3)],
        "residual SD": [round(mixed_residual_sd, 3)],
    }
)

print(render_table(mixed_model_summary))
IFN-associated pattern model question estimated stimulation effect standard error z statistic p-value donor baseline SD residual SD
Pattern5 stimulated mean activity vs control, accounting for donor 0.281 0.006 45.91 <0.001 0.0 0.012

Read this model as a formal companion to the sign test, not as a separate discovery. The sign test used only the direction of each donor-pair shift. The mixed model uses the donor-level activity values themselves while still accounting for the fact that control and stimulated measurements are paired within donor.

Here is how to read the mixed-model table:

  • IFN-associated pattern gives the run-specific pattern label being tested. In the selected R run, this is Pattern4.
  • Model question states the comparison being estimated: stimulated mean activity versus control mean activity, while accounting for donor.
  • Estimated stimulation effect is the estimated average stim - control difference after the model accounts for donor baselines. A positive value means stimulated aliquots have higher IFN-associated activity on average. Here, 0.281 is nearly identical to the simple donor-paired mean shift above, which is reassuring.
  • Standard error summarizes the uncertainty around that estimated stimulation effect. A small standard error relative to the estimate means the donor-level shifts are very consistent.
  • T statistic in R, or z statistic in Python, is the estimated stimulation effect divided by its standard error. A large positive value means the estimated stimulation effect is much larger than its estimated uncertainty.
  • P-value tests the model-based null idea that the average stimulation effect is zero after accounting for donor. The value <0.001 is consistent with a strong positive stimulation-associated shift in this dataset.
  • Donor baseline SD summarizes how much the fitted donor baselines vary after condition is included. A value near zero means the donor-level baseline differences are small in this summarized table.
  • Residual SD summarizes the remaining donor-condition variation after the model accounts for condition and donor. Smaller residual variation means the donor-level points sit close to the fitted model.

The main result is the estimated stimulation effect. A positive effect of about 0.281 means that, after donor pairing is accounted for, the selected R IFN-associated pattern has higher average activity in IFN-beta-stimulated aliquots than in matched control aliquots. This points in the same direction as the paired sign test, which strengthens the conclusion that the IFN-associated activity shift is not caused by one donor alone.

With only eight donor pairs, the p-value should still be interpreted as a compact check inside this dataset rather than as a broad clinical inference. The useful message is the agreement across evidence types: paired direction, estimated effect size, and biological gene support all point toward the same stimulation-associated pattern.

Compare Activity With A Canonical ISG Score

The IFN-associated pattern should not only separate stimulated and control cells. Its activity should also agree with known interferon biology. One simple way to check that is to build a small score from canonical , often called ISGs.

This is a teaching check, not a new cell-type annotation. The short list below is a compact guidepost drawn from interferon-response resources rather than a new signature discovered in this case study. Many of the genes appear in the MSigDB Hallmark interferon-response gene sets, and Interferome provides a broader catalog of interferon-regulated genes (Liberzon et al. 2015; Rusinova et al. 2013). The Kang source study supplies the IFN-beta PBMC perturbation context, while the lupus/interferon literature explains why an interferon-gene score is relevant in SLE (Kang et al. 2018; Catalina et al. 2019; Chyuan, Tzeng, and Chen 2019).

The code below turns that biological guidepost into a small, checkable table. Both tabs do the same four things. First, the code defines the compact ISG list. Second, it checks which of those genes are actually present in the prepared single-cell dataset. Third, it averages the expression of the available ISGs within each cell, producing one ISG score per cell. Fourth, it compares that per-cell ISG score with the run-specific IFN-associated CoGAPS activity. In the selected R run, that activity comes from Pattern4; in the Python output, it comes from the matched IFN-associated pattern for that implementation.

In the R tab, intersect() keeps only genes that appear in both the ISG list and the SingleCellExperiment row names. SummarizedExperiment::assay(sce_cells, "X") pulls out the prepared expression matrix, and colMeans() averages the selected ISG expression values across genes for each cell. The final cor(..., method = "spearman") call compares ranked ISG scores with ranked CoGAPS activity values, so the check asks whether cells with higher ISG expression also tend to have higher IFN-associated pattern activity.

The Python tab follows the same logic with AnnData and pandas. A list comprehension keeps genes found in adata_cells.var_names, slicing adata_cells[:, isg_genes_present].X pulls out the expression values, and mean(axis=1) averages those genes within each cell. The .rank().corr(...) step performs the same Spearman-style comparison by correlating the ranks of the ISG score and the ranks of the IFN-associated pattern activity.

  • R
  • Python
canonical_isg_genes_r <- c(
  # Compact IFN-response guidepost; not an exhaustive ISG database.
  "ISG15", "ISG20", "IFI6", "IFIT1", "IFIT2", "IFIT3",
  "IRF7", "MX1", "OAS1", "BST2", "PLSCR1", "LY6E",
  "TNFSF10", "RSAD2", "CXCL10", "IFITM3", "APOBEC3A"
)

isg_genes_present_r <- intersect(canonical_isg_genes_r, rownames(sce_cells))

isg_expression_r <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(sce_cells, "X")[
  isg_genes_present_r,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
isg_score_r <- colMeans(as.matrix(isg_expression_r))

shared_isg_cells_r <- intersect(names(isg_score_r), rownames(P_r))
isg_activity_corr_r <- suppressWarnings(cor(
  isg_score_r[shared_isg_cells_r],
  P_r[shared_isg_cells_r, ifn_pattern_r],
  method = "spearman"
))

isg_activity_summary_r <- tibble::tibble(
  check = c(
    "canonical ISG genes requested",
    "canonical ISG genes present",
    "cells compared",
    "Spearman correlation with IFN-associated activity"
  ),
  value = c(
    as.character(length(canonical_isg_genes_r)),
    as.character(length(isg_genes_present_r)),
    format(length(shared_isg_cells_r), big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%.3f", isg_activity_corr_r)
  )
)

knitr::kable(isg_activity_summary_r, col.names = c("Check", "Value"))

canonical_isg_genes = [
    # Compact IFN-response guidepost; not an exhaustive ISG database.
    "ISG15", "ISG20", "IFI6", "IFIT1", "IFIT2", "IFIT3",
    "IRF7", "MX1", "OAS1", "BST2", "PLSCR1", "LY6E",
    "TNFSF10", "RSAD2", "CXCL10", "IFITM3", "APOBEC3A",
]

isg_genes_present = [gene for gene in canonical_isg_genes if gene in adata_cells.var_names]
isg_matrix = adata_cells[:, isg_genes_present].X
if sparse.issparse(isg_matrix):
    isg_matrix = isg_matrix.toarray()
isg_score = pd.Series(
    np.asarray(isg_matrix).mean(axis=1),
    index=adata_cells.obs_names,
    name="canonical_isg_score",
)

shared_isg_cells = isg_score.index.intersection(P_py.index)
isg_activity_corr = (
    isg_score.loc[shared_isg_cells].rank()
    .corr(P_py.loc[shared_isg_cells, ifn_pattern_py].rank())
)

isg_activity_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Check": [
            "canonical ISG genes requested",
            "canonical ISG genes present",
            "cells compared",
            "Spearman correlation with IFN-associated activity",
        ],
        "Value": [
            str(len(canonical_isg_genes)),
            str(len(isg_genes_present)),
            f"{len(shared_isg_cells):,}",
            f"{isg_activity_corr:.3f}",
        ],
    }
)
